21 A distant star is receding from the Earth with a speed of 1.40 × 107
m s–1. It emits light of
frequency 4.57 × 1014
Hz. The speed of light is 3.00 × 108
m s–1.
The Doppler effect formula can be used with light waves.
What will be the frequency of this light when detected on Earth?
A
2.04 × 1013
Hz
B
4.37 × 1014
Hz
C
4.57 × 1014
Hz
D
4.79 × 1014
Hz

hints: Notice the star is receding at $1.40 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ while emitting $4.57 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, so the detected light must be redshifted to longer wavelength and lower frequency.
Recall the source-receding Doppler formula $f_o = f_s c/(c+v_s)$, or equivalently $\Delta f / f_s \approx v_s/c$ for $v_s$ much smaller than $c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Calculate the fractional shift $v_s/c \approx 0.0467$, then subtract the shift $f_s v_s/c$ from $4.57 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ to get the observed value.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: source receding with $v_s = 1.40 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, emitted $f_s = 4.57 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, wave speed $c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the rule: for a receding source the observed wavelength is stretched and observed frequency is reduced, $f_o = f_s \times c/(c+v_s)$.
Calculate the frequency shift: $\Delta f = f_s \times v_s/c \approx 4.57 \times 10^{14} \times 0.0467 \approx 0.213 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.
Subtract because it is receding: $f_o = f_s - \Delta f \approx 4.57 \times 10^{14} - 0.20 \times 10^{14} \approx 4.37 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ with unit $\text{Hz}$.

A.explanation: This is about $2.13 \times 10^{13} \text{ Hz}$, the size of the frequency shift $\Delta f$, not the observed frequency $f - \Delta f$.

B.explanation: A receding source gives a redshift to slightly lower frequency, $f_o = f_s c/(c+v_s) \approx 4.37 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.

C.explanation: This is the emitted frequency $4.57 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ with no Doppler shift applied, but the receding star must shift the light.

D.explanation: This is higher than the emitted frequency, which would be a blueshift for an approaching source, not a receding source.
